content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presented a method for motion isolation for dynamic medical imaging data. Specifically, the method used untrained generator networks as latent priors, and attempted to perform latent space disentanglement with some existing information on the underlying dynamics. The method is validated on synthetic phantom dataset and cardiac MR images.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- Applying motion isolation with untrained generator networks as priors is an interesting motivation (as there might exist little data for pre-training), and the application on medical imaging datasets is interesting.

Weaknesses

1. Major concern 1: the evaluation of the presented methodology is poorly conducted
- The synthetic phantom dataset is way too simple. Even the cardiac MR images seem like a relatively simple dataset.
- There are no quantitative disentanglement measurements, although the method is claimed to perform disentanglement. There are many existing metrics (e.g. MIG, MIG-sup) that can be used for measuring disentanglement.
- There is no benchmark model. It is impossible to evaluate the model’s performance when there are no other benchmark models presented.

2. Major concern 2: The methodology lacks novelty.
- The idea of the methodology highly overlaps with Ulyanov et al. (2020) deep image prior.
- Isolating motions based on sparse latent coding, with existing information about the underlying dynamics can hardly be considered novel as well. I suggest the authors check [1-4]. There are many existing unsupervised disentanglement works that enforce sparse latents.

3. Major concern 3: Related works is worryingly lacking
- Page 2 “But again, also in the context of GANs, to the best knowledge of the authors, a method capable of isolating different motion types in video data as the one proposed here does not exist.” This is not true. There are many VAE/GAN that perform disentanglement for video data. Check [5-8].
- The related works about latent disentanglement are missing.


Minor comments:
- Page3 second line $A_t \in \mathcal{L}\left(\mathbb{R}^{N_1 \times N_2}, \mathbb{R}^{\dot{M}}\right)$ is a slightly confusing notation. $\mathcal{L}$ is typically used to denote loss function. $A_t: \mathbb{R}^{N_1 \times N_2} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^{\dot{M}}$ might be a more approachable notation (as used in below generator networks G).
- Equation 2 in $\theta_j^i \in \Theta$, is $\Theta$ defined in the main text?

[1] Locatello, Francesco, et al. "Challenging common assumptions in the unsupervised learning of disentangled representations." international conference on machine learning. PMLR, 2019.

[2] Higgins, Irina, et al. "beta-vae: Learning basic visual concepts with a constrained variational framework." (2016).

[3] Kim, Hyunjik, and Andriy Mnih. "Disentangling by factorising." International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2018.

[4] Chen, Ricky TQ, et al. "Isolating sources of disentanglement in variational autoencoders." Advances in neural information processing systems 31 (2018).

[5] Zhu, Yizhe, et al. "S3vae: Self-supervised sequential vae for representation disentanglement and data generation." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2020.

[6] Denton, Emily L. "Unsupervised learning of disentangled representations from video." Advances in neural information processing systems 30 (2017).

[7] Villegas, Ruben, et al. "Decomposing motion and content for natural video sequence prediction." arXiv preprint arXiv:1706.08033 (2017).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The quality and the novelty are both low. The clarity is okay, as the presented method is simple.
content.summary_of_the_review: I suggest rejection for this paper. There barely exists any quantitative method evaluation, and the novelty of the method is very low.

content.title: Author response
content.comment:
Thank you for your review. Please note that our method does not rely on training on a data set, but rather uses an untrained model directly on a single datum (in the same spirit as the deep image prior cited in our work). We believe that this is already clearly stated in the abstract.

As consequence, we emphasize that in our opinion none of the provided references detracts from the novelty of our approach beyond what we have already stated in the introduction, and none of them provides a method that would be applicable in any way in our setting.

Additionally, main differences of our method to the provided references include: i) None of the provided references decomposes different types of motion. Those that deal with videos only decompose content and pose/motion, with the aim of predicting future frames. ii) None of the provided references deals with data from medical imaging and MRI.

Our response to the additional comments is as follows:

> There are no quantitative disentanglement measurements, although the method is claimed to perform disentanglement. There are many existing metrics (e.g. MIG, MIG-sup) that can be used for measuring disentanglement.

We do quantify the motion decomposition obtained with our method, see Table 1. The proposed metrics are not applicable in our setting, since we do not propose a method for learning disentangled representations for a dataset.

> There is no benchmark model. It is impossible to evaluate the model’s performance when there are no other benchmark models presented.

None of the provided reference can be used as benchmark.  As stated in the paper, we are not aware of any existing method capable of achieving the same type of (untrained) motion decomposition as our method. This is why we use the idealized scenario of having both motion triggers as reference to  compare with.

> The idea of the methodology highly overlaps with Ulyanov et al. (2020) deep image prior.

We explicitly state in the paper that that we ``follow the basic idea introduced in Ulyanov et al.". Note, however, that Ulyanov et al. only deals with still images, and has the fundamentally different goal of image reconstruction rather than motion decomposition.

> Page 2 “But again, also in the context of GANs, to the best knowledge of the authors, a method capable of isolating different motion types in video data as the one proposed here does not exist.” This is not true. There are many VAE/GAN that perform disentanglement for video data. Check [5-8].

We disagree, none of the provided references allows to isolate different types of motion in video data as done in our work. More strongly, there is still the fundamental difference that we decompose motion based on a single datum rather than a dataset.

content.title: Thank you
content.comment:
Thank you for your response. I would like to clarify my points below and justify my judgment further.

In my original review, I focused on expressing my negative opinion of the work. I would like to emphasize my original comment "Applying motion isolation with untrained generator networks as priors is an interesting motivation (as there might exist little data for pre-training), and the application on medical imaging datasets is interesting.", and emphasize that I do consider using an untrained model as an innovative approach and is the major strength of the work.

However, many of my opinions still hold with the authors' response. I would like to clarify and emphasize my points below:

1. Benchmarking. The author stated that "None of the provided reference can be used as benchmark." because none of the "existing method capable of achieving the same type of (untrained) motion decomposition as our method". While I agree with the argument itself as I do not realize any model could achieve the exact same disentanglement, I do not agree with the logic behind it (which is: because no model could perform the exact same task, we decide to not benchmark it at all). It is the authors' responsibility to show that the proposed model is good/motivational -- I can think of a few easy ways to benchmark the model (1) how does the model perform when a normal disentanglement model (e.g. beta-VAE) is trained on only a few images (let us say, 5 images)? If a beta-VAE performs better than the proposed method when trained on 5-images (I do realize this would give beta-VAE an advantage), then why one would prefer to use an untrained generator? (2) how does the model perform when it is compared with traditional analysis methods (e.g. phase/frequency-based methods) (3) would pre-training the model on synthetic motion datasets easily gives an outperforming model when compared with the proposed method? If one could generate a small collection of synthetic datasets and use minimal efforts to pre-train the model to achieve better performance, why would one prefer the proposed method?

With this being said, I realize my opinion about the lack of benchmarking is highly associated with the lack of convincing motivation (to me). imho, the lack of related experiments further impairs the motivation of the work.

2. No quantitative disentanglement measurements. I apologize for the possible misunderstanding provided in my previous review "There are many existing metrics (e.g. MIG, MIG-sup) that can be used for measuring disentanglement.". I was not suggesting the authors to directly apply MIG with the method, but was suggesting there exist many possible ways for the authors to follow the logic/sprits in disentanglement quantification methods and design better metrics to quantify the motion isolation/decomposition. I am aware of the existence of Table 1, but I find it hardly convincing how the numbers in table 1 (mean, std, mae, median) could be used to show the superiority of the method. I would recommend the authors design better metrics (that are self-explanatory, for example, accuracy has a range from [0, 100] and one could easily tell the performance based on a given score. Could the motion decomposition be measured similarly?) to support the evaluation.

3. Experiments are too simple. The authors did not address my comments on the difficulty of the proposed experiments. Again, upon re-thinking, I think many of my comments are associated with the motivation of the paper, as I do think many existing methods can be directly applied if the experiment condition is slightly adjusted. It seems to me the authors decided to evaluate the proposed method in a very particular setting without clear motivation to me (MRI, completely untrained model, a specific set of motions existing in the dataset).

4. The lack of related works. The authors argue that they do not include many reference/related works because "none of the provided references allows ... as done in our work". I would suggest the authors include more related works, and explicitly state the difference between the proposed work and them in the revised paper. 

5. Novelty of the work. I would like to thank the authors for clearly stating "Note, however, that Ulyanov et al. only deals with still images, and has the fundamentally different goal of image reconstruction rather than motion decomposition.". This indeed is a novelty that I neglected. However, it does not change my overall opinion of the work.

To summarize, I would still suggest clear rejection for the paper because of the reasons I listed above (under the assumption that no rebuttal thus more experiments will be provided). However, I'd like to point out that my original score of 1 is indeed a bit harsh, and is not representative of the overall quality of this work, but is more of a relatively adjusted score based on the quality of the batch of paper I received.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for further clarifying the background of his judgment. In our response, our main goal was to point out that, in our opinion, the provided references do not provide a method that can achieve something similar to what our method can achieve.

Nevertheless, we agree that a lack of baseline comparison is a valid reason for being skeptical about the paper. Already anticipating this, prior to submission, we actually spent quite some thoughts on how to set up a baseline comparison. We also experimented, e.g., with registration-based methods to achieve this. Our conclusion was that, in order to have a baseline that indeed achieves non-trivial results in our setting, we would need to adapt existing methods to an extent at which they can no longer be considered as *preexisting* baseline. We believe that, with the proposed comparison to VAEs or phase/frequency-based methods, the situation would be similar. But we agree that it is our responsibility to confirm this. For a future submission of the paper we will strive to include a comparison to other possible approaches.

For the sake of completeness, we also provide a short response to the other points made by the reviewer in his response.

> No quantitative disentanglement measurements

We agree that more self-explanatory metrics might be better and we will consider including such metrics in a revision. But please note that, in our setting, the difference of the generated images with isolated motion to the corresponding ground truth images is exactly what one wants to measure in some way or the other, and different metrics would in essence measure the same thing, but possibly with a different scaling or quantification.

> Experiments are too simple

Thank you for the clarification. In a future submission, we will put more emphasis on explaining why we believe that exactly the experimental setup of our paper, i.e., untrained breathing/cardiac motion isolation for dynamic MRI (in particular when applied jointly with reconstruction, which is possible with our method in principle), is a highly relevant problem by itself.

> The lack of related works

Thank you. In a resubmission, we will expand the related works section in the introduction as suggested.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this submission, the authors tried to present a method that can disentangle unwanted motion that can be captured by one-dimensional latent representation from the dynamics that of interest for consequent analyses. Based on the presentation, the model appears to be mostly based on the similar framework of conditional auto-encoder. The authors reported the empirical results on both simulated and MR dynamic images, the latter focusing on separating respiratory and cardiac motion.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Motion disentanglement for video analysis can be an important task to achieve unbiased meaningful results, especially in biomedical imaging as one of potential targeted applications in this submission. However, the current version of the submission many need significant revision to improve presentation, make sure that the mathematical notations are correct, and more comprehensive performance validation results. 

First, there are many presentation problems in Section 2. It is not clear what is $y_t$ in the equation (1) if $x_t$ denotes the observed dynamic images. In eq. (2), it is not clear what the superscript $i$ in $\theta_j^i$ was supported to index. Why there are two sets of $\theta$'s? More critically, the most important optimization formulation in eq. (3) definitely needs to revise: based on the current math notations, only $z^1_t$ and $\theta$ are decision variables? The authors need to clearly distinguish $z$ and $\hat{z}$. Also, did the authors assumed that $A_t$ is given or at the end, the authors only tried to solve the problem (4)? If that is the case, why we would need to introduce equations (1) and (3)? Overall the presentation is very confusing and it is rare to have only half of the page describing the proposed method in typical machine learning papers. The authors may consider to clearly present what are the new methodological contributions, in particular comparing with many existing conditional generative models and be clear on what are their unique developments. 

More comprehensive experimental results may be needed to demonstrate the significance of the proposed method. Comparison with the existing methods is necessary to demonstrate the need for the new development.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: As detailed above, there are many problems in the presentation of the proposed method. The authors need to correctly present the mathematical models and may consider to clearly present what are the new methodological contributions, in particular comparing with many existing conditional generative models and be clear on what are their unique developments.
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors proposed to disentangle unwanted motion using conditional generative models but there are several issues with the presentation and experiments as detailed in the above comments. The authors may need to significantly revise the submission for their future submission.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

Thank you for your review. Please note that our method fundamentally differs from the framework of variational autoencoders in that we do not train a model on some training data set, but rather use an untrained model directly on a single datum (in the same spirit as the deep image prior cited in our work). Regarding the suggested comparison, please note that, as stated in the paper, we are not aware of any existing method capable of achieving the same type of (untrained) motion decomposition as our method. Also, none of the reviewers cited any such method. This is why we use the idealized scenario of having both motion triggers as reference to compare with.

Regarding the mentioned problems within  the presentation in Section 2: i) $y_t$ is the measured data (as stated in line 4), ii) the index of the superscript is provided in the first line after equation (2) (it distinguishes between weights and biases), iii) yes, we only optimize over $z_t^1 $ and $\theta$ in equation (3) (as stated there), iv) we carefully distinguish between variables with and without hat: the hat always indicates fixed variables that are either given or obtained as solutions of the optimization problem, v) A is the (given) forward model as stated in the fifth line of Section 2, vi) at the end, we solve problem (5) as special case of (3); this is described in the paragraph above equation (5).

We hope this clarifies some question of the reviewer regarding Section 2. In a potential revision of the paper, we will consider a further improvement of the notation in Section 2, but please note that, in our opinion, the pertinent information is already available.

content.summary_of_the_paper: Here, the authors use a generator network with time-invariant and time-varying latent codes to infer various sources of motion in video. The core idea is that all sources of motion except for one are provided to the network. Since sources of motion map onto different latent dimensions, the dimensions can be queried after training. This is proposed in the context of cardiac MRI, where one may want to separate, e.g., breathing from cardiac motion.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**


1. The manuscript is generally well-written and easy to follow.
2. While disentanglement is not a new idea, its use to infer different sources of motion is a new idea.
3. The technique could be useful in other problem domains.

**Weaknesses**


1. The evaluation of the model on synthetic data, where there is clear ground truth, could be more complete.
	1. Clearly cardiac MRI involves quasi-periodic motion of complex images, yet the synthetic evaluation was only performed using period motion of high-contrast disks. Since this is a key example with ground truth, it is essential to verify whether the model works as expected on more complex data. How does cardiac motion reconstruction scale with, e.g., contrast between disks, additive image noise, and variability in the simulated movements? 
	2. The authors should provide an argument for why the synthetic example captures the type of movements one would see in real data.
2. Lack of controls and ablation studies on real data.
	1. A few simple controls to add here might include: shuffling the respiratory information fed into the model prior to reconstruction, randomizing the cardiac motion latent dimension during the reconstruction phase, zeroing out the time-varying latent dimensions altogether.

minor


1. typos
2. figure 6A indicate that the motion triggers are learned by the model.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is well-written and straightforward to follow, and it should be readily reproducible.

While the use of disentanglement is not novel in of itself, it's use in this particular domain is. Additionally the work is technically sound, though it could be strengthened with some simple controls (see above).
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall I found the paper to be well-argued and well-written. The presented method is fairly novel and, for the most part, is technically sound. I think the ICLR audience would benefit from its publication.

content.title: Author response
content.comment:
Thank you for explicitly stating that the method is fairly novel and that the paper is well written.
The suggested extensions of our experiments are very reasonable and we will consider them for a future submission of the paper accounting, of course, for page limitations. Some details on the suggested extensions:

Temporal variations in the video are encoded by our method only in the latent variables, while no temporal correspondence of the latent variables between different frames is enforced. Therefore, we are confident that the suggested inclusion of non-periodic motion or the suggested re-shuffling of the respiratory motion, are both scenarios that can be handled by our method.

Regarding the suggested inclusion of contrast variations: We have already successfully carried out experiments with contrast changes between the disks (which would simulate perfusion imaging), but not included them in the paper due to space constraints. We will consider including them in a future resubmission.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a method to isolate different motion types in video data, given that the states of those motion types can be described as 1-dimensional time series. To the best knowledge of the authors, this is the first method that is capable of isolating different motion types in video data.

The proposed method works as follows:
1) a generator is trained directly on a single video for the reconstruction task, but the latent vector is separated into 3 parts: time-independent information, time-dependent unknown information, and time-dependent variables each describing one motion type. 
2) the generator is trained by optimizing the generator model parameter and time-dependent unknown information.  the generator learns to isolate the corresponding motion type.

content.title: Author response
content.comment:
Thank you for your review. Please note that both the *Summary* and the *Strengths and Weaknesses* sections of the review contain the same text.

Regarding the suggestion to add more test problems with a higher number of motion types, please note that there are mainly three motion types that are relevant for cardiac cine MRI: cardiac motion, respiratory motion, and motion due to patient movement. These three types of motion are already included in the experiments presented in Section A.3 in the appendix. Adding additional motion types is something we will consider for a potential future submission of the paper, but this would mean going beyond experiments for cardiac cine MRI.

Moreover, we understand from the review that we should re-write the methods section and add more details on how motion separation is evaluated. We will take these suggestions into account for a potential future submission of the paper.

content.title: Response to reviews
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their feedback on our work. However, we would like to point out that we disagree with some of the reviewers on important points, particularly points that appear to be their basis for evaluation and  decision. Most importantly, we emphasize that in our opinion none of the references cited by reviewer J3WM detracts from the novelty of our approach beyond what we have already stated in the introduction, and none of them provides a method that would be applicable in any way in our setting. More detailed responses are provided below.

In any case, we acknowledge that our work was not received very positively by the reviewers, and that chances of acceptance of the paper are very low if we carry out a revision only according to points we agree with. For this reason we will withdraw the paper at the end of the author response period on November 18. We nevertheless thank the reviewers and the section editors for their effort in handling our paper.
